title: FPV Racing: MultiGP, Gates & Classes
html:
What organized FPV racing actually is

FPV racing is timed, multi-pilot competition through a marked course of gates and flags. In the US the dominant grassroots organization is MultiGP, which runs a network of local chapters. A chapter is a group of pilots with a registered field who run sanctioned events; results upload to MultiGP's leaderboards so you can compare yourself nationally. Internationally you'll also see Drone Champions League (DCL) and MultiGP Global Qualifier series feeding bigger finals.

Race formats

  • Heat racing — 4 pilots launch together, fly a set number of laps (often 3), top finishers advance through a bracket. This is the classic spectator format.
  • Time Trial (single-pilot) — you fly the course alone for fastest lap. MultiGP's UTT (Universal Time Trial) tracks use a standardized layout so any chapter's times are comparable.
  • Endurance / Spec — same hardware for everyone to test pure piloting.

Gates and course elements

Courses mix square gates, flags (a single pole you round), ladders/hurdles (low gates you skim), and dive gates. Each pilot runs a different video channel (typically on the 5.8 GHz band) so four feeds don't interfere; race directors assign channels per heat (e.g. R1/R3/R6/R8 on RaceBand for clean separation).

Classes and the spec mindset

ClassFrame / packNotes
Spec / Open 5-inch5" prop, 6S, ~800gThe mainstream race class; raw speed
MultiGP SpecDefined motor KV, 5" tri-blade, 6S 1300mAh limitsLevels the field — skill over budget
Tiny Whoop / micro65-75mm, 1SIndoor racing, cheap entry
3-inch / Toothpick3" prop, 4SSmaller venues
Rules vary.
Class specs (motor KV, battery cell count/capacity, weight) change season to season. Always read the current MultiGP rulebook for the season you're entering, and check FAA Remote ID / registration applies to your aircraft (over 250g must be registered).

Gear you need to race

  • A reliable 6S 5-inch quad (or the spec build the class mandates) plus 1-2 backups — crashes happen.
  • Goggles with the same video format the event supports. Many chapters still run analog; digital (DJI O3/O4, Walksnail, HDZero) is growing but HDZero is favored for racing due to low latency.
  • A VTX you can set to a specific channel/power. Races usually cap power at 25mW so four pilots don't desync each other's feeds.
  • 4-6 charged race packs, a field charger, prop spares, a tool roll.

Getting involved

Make a free MultiGP account, use the chapter finder, and just show up to a practice day — most chapters welcome newcomers and many run a Spec class specifically so beginners aren't outspent. Bring a registered aircraft, your FAA registration number marked on the airframe, and ask the race director where to spawn your video channel before you ever power on the VTX.

Prop & power safety.
Never power a quad with props on while goggling up near others. Power VTX only on your assigned channel — a stray channel at full power can knock another pilot out of the air. Keep LiPos in a fire bag at the pits.
▸Hands-On

Plan to attend or enter a real race.

  1. Use the MultiGP chapter finder to locate the nearest chapter or open practice.
  2. Read its event page: identify the class offered (e.g. Spec 6S) and the video format (analog/HDZero/DJI).
  3. List the gear you must bring: aircraft + spares, goggles, VTX channel capability, packs, FAA registration marked on the frame.
  4. Write a one-paragraph plan: date, class you'll enter, and what you still need to buy or borrow.

title: The Freestyle Scene: Community, Edits & Brands
html:
What freestyle is

Freestyle is the artistic, non-competitive side of FPV: flowing lines, dives, power loops, matty flips, juicy rolls, and proximity tricks flown for the feel and the footage rather than the clock. The culture is built around the edit — a 1-3 minute video set to music that showcases a flight at a location. Pilots like Mr. Steele, Nurk, and Johnny FPV essentially defined the look that brands now chase.

How pilots build an audience

  • Consistency of vibe. The strongest channels have a recognizable style — color grade, music taste, the way they link tricks. Viewers subscribe to a feeling, not just clips.
  • Location hunting. Abandoned buildings (bandos), waterfalls, bridges, forests, snowy mountains. A great spot carries an average flight; a parking lot rarely does.
  • Posting cadence. Short-form (Reels/Shorts/TikTok) for reach, long-form (YouTube) for depth and ad revenue. Many pilots seed a 15-second hook clip to short-form and link the full edit.
  • Community. Engaging on Rotor Riot, the FPV subreddits, and local meetups builds the network that gets you noticed and invited to group sessions.

What makes an edit compelling

ElementWhat good looks like
FlowLines connect — no aimless hovering; momentum carried trick to trick
LocationDepth and scale to fly through and around (proximity)
EditCuts land on the beat; speed-ramps on dives; no clip overstays
MusicDrives pacing and emotion; track choice is half the edit
ColorConsistent grade; GoPro flat profile graded in post, not baked-in

The gear that makes footage look pro

  • An HD action cam (GoPro Hero or DJI) recording in a flat/log profile at high bitrate, graded later. Shoot at a high frame rate (60-120fps) so you can slow down dives smoothly.
  • ND filters to keep the shutter near 1/(2×fps) — this gives natural motion blur instead of the choppy, video-game look that screams amateur.
  • Gyro stabilization (GoPro's in-cam or Gyroflow with the cam's .gpmf log) to remove prop vibration and jello.

What brands actually look for

FPV brands (frame makers, VTX/camera companies, prop and motor brands, battery vendors) sponsor pilots to put product in beautiful footage in front of buyers. They evaluate:

  • Audience fit and engagement — a focused 20k-subscriber FPV channel can beat a generic 200k one.
  • Production quality — your edit is their ad.
  • Reliability and professionalism — do you post on time, represent the brand well, disclose partnerships honestly?

Most sponsorships start small: a discount code, free product, or affiliate links — not a salary. Build the body of work first; the deals follow the reach.

Insight.
The flight and the edit are two separate skills. Plenty of incredible pilots have flat channels because they never learned to cut to music. Treat editing as a craft worth its own practice time.
Fly responsibly.
Bando and proximity flying often happens near people, property, and below 400ft near structures. Respect no-fly zones, get permission for private property, and keep a spotter — a crash into a person is a lawsuit and a safety incident.
▸Hands-On

Reverse-engineer three edits you admire.

  1. Pick three freestyle edits and watch each twice.
  2. For each, write one sentence each on flow, location, edit/cut timing, and music choice.
  3. Note the single technique you could copy in your next session (a line, a grade, a cut style).
  4. Write your own one-line stylistic identity: the vibe your channel would have.

title: Aerial Photo & Video as a Business
html:
The most accessible commercial path

Aerial media is where most people first make money with a drone because the barrier is low: a stabilized camera platform (DJI Mavic/Air class), basic editing, and a Part 107 certificate. The hard part isn't flying — it's understanding what the client actually buys.

Commercial work requires Part 107.
In the US, flying a drone for any business purpose — including footage you sell, post for a client, or use in marketing — requires the FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate. Recreational rules do not cover paid work. Verify current FAA requirements (registration, Remote ID, airspace authorization via LAANC) before any job.

The three core niches

NicheClient buysReality
Real estate5-15 stills + a short walkthrough that makes a listing popVolume game; fast turnaround beats artistry; agents want it next-day
Weddings / eventsCinematic establishing shots and one hero revealOne chance, no reshoot; you support a ground videographer
Tourism / hospitalityPromotional reels of resorts, venues, destinationsHigher budgets; needs strong cinematic and color skills

What each niche really needs

  • Real estate is about reliability and speed. Agents reuse photographers who deliver bright, level, well-composed stills by the next morning. Standard package: aerial stills of the property and lot lines, a 30-60s clip, sometimes a twilight shot. Avoid neighbors' windows and stay legal on altitude.
  • Weddings are unforgiving — you get one take. Drone is a complement to the ground crew, not the main camera. Scout the venue, pre-plan the reveal shot, and have a battery-charged backup aircraft. Noise and crowds mean you fly during the right moments only.
  • Tourism rewards production value: smooth reveals, color grading, music. These clients pay more but expect a polished reel, model/property releases, and often multiple shoot days.

Settings that separate pro from hobby

  • Shoot video in a flat/D-Log color profile, grade in post. Lock shutter near double the frame rate using ND filters for natural motion.
  • Shoot stills in RAW (DNG) and bracket exposures for high-contrast scenes (bright sky, dark roof).
  • Keep moves slow and deliberate — slow reveals and orbits read as cinematic; jerky inputs read as amateur.

Building a package

A package = deliverables + turnaround + price. Define exactly what the client receives (e.g. "12 edited stills + one 45-second 1080p clip, delivered in 48 hours") so there's no scope creep. Charge for the result, not your flight time.

Safety over the shot.
Never fly over crowds without proper authorization. Maintain visual line of sight, respect the 400ft AGL limit, and check airspace — many wedding venues and downtowns sit in controlled airspace requiring LAANC authorization. A failsafe Return-to-Home should be configured before every job.
▸Hands-On

Outline a real service package for one niche.

  1. Pick one niche (real estate, weddings, or tourism).
  2. List exact deliverables (number of stills, video length/resolution).
  3. State your turnaround time and how the client receives files.
  4. Note the certification (Part 107) and any airspace authorization (LAANC) the job requires.

title: Mapping, Surveying & Photogrammetry
html:
From photos to measurable models

Photogrammetry turns hundreds of overlapping aerial photos into measurable products: orthomosaics (a flat, geo-accurate map), digital elevation/surface models (DEM/DSM), 3D point clouds, and volume calculations. Software stitches images by matching common features across overlapping frames. The paying markets are construction, surveying/GIS, mining/aggregate, and insurance.

The capture rules that make or break a map

ParameterTypical valueWhy
Front overlap75-80%Each ground point must appear in many photos to triangulate
Side overlap65-75%Prevents holes between flight lines
AltitudeSet by required GSDHigher = faster but lower resolution
Camera angleNadir (straight down) for maps; obliques for 3DObliques capture building facades
Flight patternGrid / lawnmower (crosshatch for 3D)Even, predictable coverage

GSD — the number clients care about

Ground Sample Distance is the real-world size of one pixel. A GSD of 2 cm/px means each pixel covers 2 cm on the ground — finer detail = lower flight = more photos and battery. GSD scales with altitude and sensor: roughly GSD = (sensor_pixel_size × altitude) / focal_length. Quote the deliverable in GSD (e.g. "2.5 cm/px orthomosaic") because that defines how small a feature the client can measure.

Ground control and accuracy

  • GCPs (Ground Control Points) — surveyed markers placed in the scene and tagged in software. They tie the model to real-world coordinates and dramatically improve absolute accuracy.
  • RTK/PPK drones (DJI Phantom 4 RTK, Matrice with RTK, WingtraOne) geotag each photo to centimeter accuracy, reducing or eliminating GCP needs for many jobs.
  • Surveyors often require both: RTK for the bulk plus a few checkpoints to verify accuracy.

Processing software

  • Pix4Dmapper / Pix4Dmatic — survey-grade, widely accepted.
  • DroneDeploy — cloud, easy, strong for construction progress.
  • Agisoft Metashape — powerful, one-time license, great 3D.
  • Esri Site Scan / ArcGIS — when the client lives in a GIS ecosystem.

What a construction client expects

Construction wants actionable, repeatable data: a georeferenced orthomosaic they can drop into Civil 3D or ArcGIS, a DSM, cut/fill volume reports for earthwork, and progress comparison against the design surface. Many sites are flown weekly. Deliver in their CRS (coordinate reference system) — get this in writing before you fly, because a model in the wrong projection is useless.

Insight.
The flight is 20% of the job. The value is in clean, accurate, correctly-projected deliverables. A surveyor will not accept "pretty" — they need documented accuracy (RMSE on checkpoints) and the right datum.
Verify scope.
Selling survey data may intersect with state surveying/licensure laws — in some jurisdictions producing legal boundary or survey-grade deliverables requires a licensed surveyor. Confirm what you're legally allowed to deliver and partner with a licensed surveyor when needed. Part 107 still applies for the flying.
▸Hands-On

Outline a mapping job for a construction client.

  1. State the site size and the target GSD (e.g. 2.5 cm/px) and back-calculate the altitude.
  2. Specify front/side overlap and flight pattern (grid vs crosshatch).
  3. Decide GCP vs RTK and how you'll verify accuracy (checkpoints).
  4. Pick processing software and list the exact deliverables (orthomosaic, DSM, volume report) and the CRS.

title: Precision Agriculture: Crop Health & Spraying
html:
Two distinct ag drone businesses

Agricultural drones split into two very different services: data/scouting (mapping crop health with multispectral imagery) and application/spraying (heavy-lift drones that apply pesticide, fertilizer, or seed). They use different aircraft, different licensing, and serve different parts of the grower's budget.

Crop-health mapping and NDVI

A multispectral camera (e.g. MicaSense RedEdge, DJI Mavic 3 Multispectral) captures bands beyond visible light — notably near-infrared (NIR) and red. Healthy plants reflect a lot of NIR and absorb red light for photosynthesis; stressed plants reflect less NIR. The NDVI index makes this visible:

NDVI
NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red) +0.6 to +0.9 dense, healthy canopy +0.2 to +0.5 sparse / stressed vegetation below 0.1 bare soil, water, or dead crop

The output is a color-coded field map showing where crops are stressed before the eye can see it. Other indices (NDRE for later-season nitrogen, VARI from a normal RGB camera as a cheap proxy) target specific problems.

The value to the grower

  • Early detection of irrigation failures, pest/disease hotspots, and nutrient deficiency — days or weeks before visible symptoms.
  • Variable-rate prescriptions — the map drives a prescription so the farmer applies fertilizer/water only where needed, cutting input cost.
  • Stand counts and damage assessment after weather events (useful for insurance claims).

Spraying drones

Heavy-lift sprayers like the DJI Agras T40/T50 carry 40-50L tanks and apply chemicals over terrain that's too wet, steep, or dense for a ground rig. Advantages: no soil compaction, access to flooded/hilly fields, and less operator chemical exposure. They fly autonomous swaths following a terrain-aware map.

Spraying needs more than Part 107.
Applying chemicals from a drone in the US typically requires a Part 137 Agricultural Aircraft Operator certificate, often a Part 44807 / exemption for aircraft over 55 lbs, plus a state pesticide applicator license. This is a serious regulatory and safety undertaking — verify current FAA and state rules before offering it.

The ROI pitch

Growers buy outcomes, not technology. Frame it in dollars per acre: if a $X/acre scouting flight finds an irrigation failure or a $Y/acre nitrogen overspend across a 200-acre field, the savings dwarf the service fee. Repeat business comes from delivering maps fast (same-day) and in a format their agronomist already uses.

Chemical & flight safety.
Spray drones carry tens of kilos of liquid and large props — they are dangerous aircraft. Use PPE for chemical handling, never spray in wind that causes drift onto people/neighbors, and follow the chemical label (the label is the law). Maintain failsafe behavior so a lost link doesn't dump a tank uncontrolled.
▸Hands-On

Write a one-page pitch for one ag service.

  1. Pick crop-health (NDVI) mapping.
  2. Explain what you capture (multispectral) and the output (color stress map + prescription).
  3. Quantify the ROI: per-acre fee vs the input cost or yield loss it prevents.
  4. State turnaround and the file format you'll hand the grower's agronomist.

title: Infrastructure Inspection: Roofs, Solar, Towers & Wind
html:
Why inspection is a strong business

Drones replace people on ropes, scaffolds, and bucket trucks. They cut inspection cost and time and remove humans from height — that safety case is what sells the service to insurers, utilities, and facility managers. The work is recurring (assets are re-inspected) and the deliverable is a documented report, not just pretty footage.

The four core asset types

AssetWhat you look forSensor
RoofsHail/storm damage, missing shingles, membrane tears, pondingRGB + sometimes thermal for trapped moisture
Solar farmsDead cells, hot spots, string failures, soilingThermal (radiometric) + RGB
Cell / comm towersAntenna count/azimuth, corrosion, bolt/connector conditionHigh-res RGB + zoom
Wind turbinesBlade cracks, leading-edge erosion, lightning damageHigh-res RGB, sometimes thermal

Workflows

  • Roofs — fly a grid for an orthomosaic to document the whole roof, then oblique close-ups of damage. Thermal at dusk reveals moisture under the membrane (wet insulation holds heat). Insurance clients want time-stamped, geotagged images per defect.
  • Solar — fly an automated grid at fixed altitude with a radiometric thermal camera (e.g. DJI Mavic 3T / Matrice with H20T). Hot spots show as bright points; whole-string failures show as dark rows. Software (e.g. solar-specific analytics) maps each anomaly to a panel ID and IEC fault category. Fly when irradiance is high (sunny, panels under load) for thermal contrast.
  • Towers — orbit at multiple heights capturing antennas and structure; zoom cameras keep you at a safe standoff. Deliver an antenna/azimuth report and a defect log.
  • Wind turbines — the turbine must be stopped and locked before flight. Fly each blade's four faces (leading edge, trailing edge, suction, pressure sides), capturing systematic overlapping shots so each meter of blade is documented.
Proximity flying is the real risk.
Inspection means flying close to metal structures that wreck GPS and compass (magnetic interference) and create turbulence/rotor downwash. Expect GPS dropouts near towers and solar racking — be ready to fly in ATTI/manual and keep a safe standoff. Brief everyone on the lockout for wind turbines, never fly over live energized lines closer than required, and maintain a spotter at all times.

Data and deliverables

Clients buy a report: an annotated set of images, each tagged with location/defect type/severity, often in their asset-management system. Consistency matters — same altitude, same overlap, same angles every visit so year-over-year comparison is valid. For solar, a radiometric (temperature-measuring) thermal sensor is essential; a non-radiometric camera can't give the °C deltas the analysis needs.

Insight.
The differentiator isn't the flight — it's repeatability and reporting. Build a fixed flight template per asset so every inspection is comparable and defensible in an insurance dispute.
▸Hands-On

Build an inspection checklist for one asset.

  1. Choose a roof or a solar array.
  2. Define the flight pattern (grid altitude + overlap, plus oblique close-ups).
  3. List the data captured (RGB, radiometric thermal) and how each defect is tagged.
  4. Write the safety steps: airspace check, GPS-interference plan, spotter, standoff distance, and (for solar) the irradiance/time-of-day requirement.

title: Public Safety, Search-and-Rescue & Light Shows
html:
Drones in public safety

Police, fire, and emergency-management agencies use drones as a fast, cheap eye in the sky. Common missions: search and rescue (SAR), fire scene size-up and hot-spot detection, crash/crime scene mapping, hazmat standoff, crowd monitoring, and DFR (Drone as First Responder) programs where a drone launches from a rooftop dock to a 911 call before officers arrive.

What makes SAR work

  • Thermal imaging — a radiometric or high-sensitivity thermal camera (e.g. DJI Matrice 30T / M3T) finds a body-heat signature in woods, fields, or water at night when human searchers can't see.
  • Loudspeaker and spotlight payloads to communicate with or locate a subject.
  • Systematic search grids flown autonomously so no area is missed, coordinated with ground teams over the same map.
  • Endurance and reliability — enterprise platforms with redundant systems, IP-rated for rain, and long flight times matter far more than camera prettiness.
Operating authority varies.
Public agencies in the US can fly under a Certificate of Authorization (COA) or under Part 107. Night and BVLOS SAR work often needs waivers/authorizations. Programs must coordinate with manned aircraft (a medevac helicopter shares that airspace). Always verify current FAA rules and local emergency-operations protocols.

Roles in a public-safety drone program

  • Remote pilot in command (RPIC) — flies and is legally responsible.
  • Visual observer — keeps eyes on the aircraft and airspace.
  • Payload/sensor operator — runs the camera and interprets imagery.
  • Mission coordinator — links the drone feed to incident command and ground teams.

Drone light shows

Light shows replace fireworks with swarms of hundreds or thousands of small LED drones flying choreographed 3D animations. They're quiet, reusable, and programmable — a growing business for events, sports, and brand activations (companies like Sky Elements, Verge Aero, Intel/SPHEREO-style operators run them).

How a light show is produced

  1. Design — animators build the 3D animation in specialized software (e.g. Verge Aero, Skybrush/Blender), where each drone is one moving pixel.
  2. Choreography to music — the timeline is synced to an audio track.
  3. Path planning & collision checks — software verifies no two drones intersect and that each stays within geofence and battery limits.
  4. Show drones — small, GPS/RTK-guided quads with bright RGB LEDs, launched from a grid and flown fully autonomously from a single ground control station.
  5. Operations crew — show designer, flight operations lead, safety officer, ground crew for launch/recovery and battery swaps.
Swarm safety.
Hundreds of aircraft over a crowd demand redundancy: precise RTK positioning, automated geofencing, and a one-button abort that lands the fleet safely. Operating over people requires specific FAA authorization. Reliable LiPo handling and pre-flight checks across the whole fleet are non-negotiable.
▸Hands-On

Research one public-safety program and one light-show op.

  1. Find a real public-safety/SAR drone program; list its aircraft, sensors (thermal?), and crew roles.
  2. Find a real light-show operator; list the drone type, software, and crew roles.
  3. Note the regulatory authority each operates under (COA/Part 107, operations-over-people waiver).
  4. Summarize in a short table comparing equipment and roles.

title: Delivery & Emerging Markets
html:
The state of drone delivery

Drone delivery has moved from demo to limited commercial reality. The leaders carry small payloads short distances — food, medicine, retail items — and win where speed beats road traffic. Notable operations:

OperatorModelNotes
ZiplineFixed-wing + droid that lowers package on a tetherStarted with medical/blood delivery in Rwanda; now US retail/health
Wing (Alphabet)Hover-and-winch from a small VTOLSuburban food/retail, e.g. parts of the US and Australia
Amazon Prime AirMultirotor, drops in backyardLimited markets; slow regulatory ramp
DroneUp / FlytrexMultirotor partnered with retailersSuburban grocery/restaurant

Why it's hard — the BVLOS wall

Economic delivery requires flying beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) — one operator can't deliver at scale while keeping eyes on the aircraft. Standard Part 107 requires visual line of sight, so every meaningful delivery operation needs a BVLOS waiver or exemption, which is slow and demanding to obtain.

The regulatory hurdles

  • BVLOS authorization — historically granted case-by-case via Part 107 waivers or Part 135 air-carrier certification (Zipline and Wing hold Part 135 certificates to operate as actual airlines).
  • Detect-and-avoid (DAA) — the aircraft must sense and avoid other traffic without a human watching; regulators require proof.
  • UTM / airspace integration — Unmanned Traffic Management to deconflict many drones in low airspace.
  • Remote ID — broadcast identification is now required and underpins accountability.
  • Community acceptance — noise and privacy concerns shape where operations are allowed.
Rules are actively changing.
The FAA's long-awaited Part 108 BVLOS rulemaking aims to create a standardized path so operators don't need bespoke waivers. Status and details evolve — always check the current FAA rulemaking and your local aviation authority before assuming what's permitted.

Other emerging markets

  • Medical/logistics — moving lab samples, organs, and pharmacy items between facilities.
  • Drone-in-a-box / docking — autonomous aircraft living in a weatherproof dock for security patrol, DFR, and recurring site monitoring with no pilot on site.
  • Counter-UAS and detection — a growing security market.
  • Heavy-lift cargo and agricultural application — larger payload aircraft.
Insight.
The opportunity for most small operators isn't running a delivery airline — it's the support ecosystem: docking-site setup, BVLOS waiver consulting, fleet maintenance, and being a certified pilot/ops staff for the companies that hold the certificates.
▸Hands-On

Summarize the delivery landscape and its barriers.

  1. Pick two current delivery operations (e.g. Zipline and Wing).
  2. For each, note payload, delivery mechanism, and where they operate.
  3. List the regulatory barriers each had to clear (BVLOS authorization, Part 135 vs Part 107 waiver, detect-and-avoid, Remote ID).
  4. Write one sentence on a realistic way a small operator could participate in this market.

title: Making Money: Services, Pricing, Content, Racing & Teaching
html:
The revenue paths, honestly ranked

PathMoney realityBest for
Services (media, mapping, inspection)Most reliable income; B2B pays wellPeople who want a real business
Content / YouTubeSlow to build; long tail via ads, affiliate, brand dealsStrong editors with patience
RacingRarely profitable; prizes + sponsorship are thinPassion-driven, builds your brand
Selling built dronesMargins thin solo; better as repair/custom buildsSkilled builders/solderers
Teaching / Part 107 prepHigh margin; scalable as coursesPeople who can explain clearly

The biggest pricing mistake

Beginners price by "how long the flight took" and undercharge to near minimum wage. You sell a result and assume the business risk — insurance, gear depreciation, editing time, travel, no-show risk, and the years of skill that let you deliver reliably. Price the whole job.

What goes into a real quote

  • On-site time — drive, setup, flight, teardown (often 3-4× the actual flight time).
  • Post-production — editing/processing is usually the largest time block.
  • Gear amortization — a slice of your aircraft, batteries, cameras, software subscriptions, and computer.
  • Travel — mileage and time.
  • Licensing & insurance — Part 107, liability insurance per job/year, software licenses (Pix4D/DroneDeploy).
  • Overhead + profit — your business doesn't run for free; add margin.

Worked example: a real-estate shoot

quote — real estate aerials
Deliverable: 12 edited stills + 45s clip, 48h turnaround On-site (drive+setup+fly+teardown) 2.0 h Editing (stills + clip) 2.5 h Travel 25 mi --- itemized --- Labor 4.5 h @ $90/h ............... $405 Travel 25 mi @ $0.67 .............. $17 Gear/software amortization ........ $30 LAANC/airspace admin .............. $0 (uncontrolled) Subtotal ......................... $452 Round to package price Flat package: $450

Note you don't show the client the hourly breakdown — you quote a clean $450 package. The breakdown is for you, to be sure the package covers cost plus profit. For mapping or inspection, the same method applies but add processing hours, GCP time, and software seat cost — those jobs price into the four-figure range.

Insight.
Productize. "Aerial Listing Package - $450" closes faster than a custom quote every time, and it stops you negotiating against yourself. Have a Basic / Standard / Premium tier so clients choose how much, not whether.

Stacking income streams

The pros rarely live on one stream. A media shooter teaches a weekend Part 107 prep course; a racer runs an affiliate-linked YouTube channel; an inspection pilot sells a notion template of their checklists. One skill set, several monetizations.

Stay legal.
All paid flying needs Part 107 and a registered aircraft; carry liability insurance; check airspace (LAANC) for every job. Verify current FAA rules before quoting work you're not yet certified or insured to perform.
Pre-flight every paid job.
A crash on a client site is a liability event. Run a checklist: props/battery condition, GPS lock, RTH altitude set above obstacles, failsafe configured, airspace clear. Never let the pressure of a paid shoot push you past safe limits or weather.
▸Hands-On

Price one real job end-to-end and plan a second stream.

  1. Pick a job (real-estate shoot or a roof/solar inspection).
  2. Itemize: on-site time, post-production, travel, gear amortization, licensing/insurance.
  3. Add margin and round to a clean package price you'd quote the client.
  4. Write one line describing a second income stream you'd add (e.g. teach a Part 107 prep workshop) using the same skills.
